flashcard_questions.q: Why do giant ionic lattices have high melting and boiling points?
flashcard_questions.a: A lot of energy is needed to overcome the many strong electrostatic forces between oppositely charged ions.

flashcard_questions.q: Why does an ionic compound not conduct electricity when it is solid?
flashcard_questions.a: Its ions are held in fixed positions, so they cannot move to carry charge.

flashcard_questions.q: When is an ionic compound able to conduct electricity?
flashcard_questions.a: When molten or dissolved in water, because the ions are then free to move.

flashcard_questions.q: What is overcome when a simple covalent substance melts or boils?
flashcard_questions.a: The weak intermolecular forces between the molecules, not the covalent bonds inside them.

flashcard_questions.q: Why do simple covalent substances not conduct electricity?
flashcard_questions.a: They have no free electrons or ions to carry charge.

flashcard_questions.q: Why are polymers usually solid at room temperature?
flashcard_questions.a: Their long chains touch at many points, so the intermolecular forces between them are strong.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is an alloy harder and stronger than a pure metal?
flashcard_questions.a: Atoms of different sizes distort the regular layers, so the layers cannot slide over each other.

flashcard_questions.q: How many covalent bonds does each carbon atom form in diamond?
Why does diamond not conduct electricity?
flashcard_questions.a: All four outer electrons on each carbon atom are used in bonding, so none are free.

flashcard_questions.q: How many other carbon atoms does each carbon atom bond to in graphite?
Why does graphite conduct electricity even though it is a non-metal?
flashcard_questions.a: Each carbon atom has one delocalised electron that is free to move along the layers.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is graphite soft and slippery enough to use as a lubricant?
flashcard_questions.a: Weak intermolecular forces hold its layers together, so they slide over each other easily.

flashcard_questions.q: What is graphene, in terms of the structure of graphite?
flashcard_questions.a: A single layer of graphite, just one atom thick.

flashcard_questions.q: How many carbon atoms are there in a molecule of buckminsterfullerene?
What is meant by allotropes of an element?
flashcard_questions.a: Different structural forms of the same element in the same physical state.

notes: 15 cards: 3 term→definition (graphene, allotropes, what melts in a simple molecule), 6 structure-to-property cards (ionic lattice, diamond, graphite, alloy, polymer), 2 value cards (four bonds in diamond, three in graphite, C₆₀), 4 conductivity 'why' cards that separate ionic, simple covalent, diamond and graphite so they do not interfere. Dropped sublimation, the melting/boiling-point state rule, monomers and carbon nanotubes to stay inside 15; the lesson's title topics (structure, properties, allotropes) were prioritised.
